stem: A 68-year-old man with Parkinson's disease (on levodopa/carbidopa 100/25mg TDS) develops gradually worsening visual hallucinations over 4 weeks — seeing small animals in his peripheral vision and people standing in doorways. He finds them distressing. His cognition is intact (MoCA 27/30). He has no delusions, no mood disturbance, and is sleeping poorly. Which is the MOST appropriate FIRST step?
options: Start quetiapine 12.5mg nocte
Start clozapine 12.5mg BD
Reduce levodopa dose by 50% and refer to neurology

Check for infection, electrolyte disturbance, constipation, and consider if medications can be REDUCED (first reduce anticholinergics, then dopamine agonists, then COMT inhibitors) before adding an antipsychotic
Start risperidone 0.5mg daily
distractors_rationale: Quetiapine is FIRST-LINE antipsychotic for PDP (lowest EPS risk) but should NOT be the FIRST step. Medication optimisation should precede antipsychotic initiation. NICE NG71: 'Offer antipsychotics only after other measures have failed.'
Clozapine is SECOND-LINE for PDP (if quetiapine fails). It is effective but requires blood monitoring. Not first-line and not the first step.

Reducing levodopa by 50% risks significant motor deterioration. The correct sequence is: (1) Reduce anticholinergics (if prescribed); (2) Reduce dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) — HIGHEST psychosis risk; (3) Reduce COMT inhibitors (entacapone); (4) LASTLY, if necessary, reduce levodopa (lowest psychosis risk of all PD meds).

CORRECT. NICE NG71 (Parkinson's disease) and Maudsley Guidelines provide a STEPWISE approach: STEP 1: Rule out physical causes (infection, constipation, dehydration, electrolyte). STEP 2: REVIEW MEDICATIONS — reduce in this order: (a) Anticholinergics (e.g., trihexyphenidyl) — these can cause confusion and hallucinations; (b) Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole — highest psychosis risk, up to 30-40%); (c) COMT inhibitors (entacapone); (d) MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline); (e) LAST — reduce levodopa (the most effective for motor symptoms, lowest psychosis risk). If medication reduction resolves psychosis and the patient is not distressed, no further treatment is needed. STEP 3: If psychosis persists despite optimisation: start QUETIAPINE (12.5-75mg nightly). Start low (12.5mg) and go slow.

Risperidone is CONTRAINDICATED in Parkinson's disease psychosis (PDP). It causes significant dopamine blockade (D2) that will WORSEN PARKINSONISM. The classic teaching: Parkinson's patients are EXQUISITELY SENSITIVE to D2 antagonism — risperidone (and haloperidol, olanzapine) can cause severe rigidity, bradykinesia, and immobility.
teaching_point: Parkinson's disease psychosis (PDP) — MANAGEMENT ALGORITHM: (1) Assess for medical causes (infection, electrolyte, constipation, dehydration). (2) Simplify medication regimen (reduce in order: anticholinergics > dopamine agonists > COMT-I > MAO-B-I > LAST — levodopa). (3) If symptoms persist and are distressing — ADD QUETIAPINE (12.5-75mg) FIRST-LINE. (4) If quetiapine fails or not tolerated — CLOZAPINE (12.5-50mg) SECOND-LINE (effective but FBC monitoring required). (5) AVOID: risperidone, olanzapine, haloperidol — all worsen parkinsonism. PIMAVANSERIN (5-HT2A inverse agonist) — licensed in the US for PDP but not widely available in UK. Prevalence: up to 40% of PD patients develop psychosis. Risk factors: disease duration, age, cognitive impairment, dopamine agonist use. The hallucinations often start as 'BENIGN' (insight preserved) but can become malignant (loss of insight, delusions, distress).
source: NICE NG71: Parkinson's disease; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; BNF

stem:
Theme: Alcohol Withdrawal Syndromes

For each clinical scenario, select the CORRECT SYNDROME:

A. Alcohol withdrawal seizure (rum fits)
B. Alcoholic hallucinosis
C. Delirium tremens
D. Wernicke's encephalopathy
E. Korsakoff's syndrome
F. Pathological intoxication
G. Idiosyncratic alcohol intoxication
H. Alcohol amnestic disorder
I. Alcohol-induced psychotic disorder
J. Alcohol-induced dementia
options: A 45-year-old man develops auditory hallucinations overnight voices threatening him 36 hours after his last drink. He is oriented, has a clear consciousness, and has no tremor or autonomic instability.

A 52-year-old man on day 3 of alcohol detoxification becomes acutely confused, agitated, with visual hallucinations (seeing spiders on the walls), tachycardia 120bpm, hypertension 160/95, and fever 37.8°C. He is disoriented to time and place.
A 38-year-old man who stopped drinking 12 hours ago has a GENERALISED TONIC-CLONIC SEIZURE lasting 2 minutes. He has no history of epilepsy.
A 50-year-old man with chronic alcohol dependence and poor nutrition presents with acute confusion, ataxia, and bilateral horizontal nystagmus. He is disoriented and has difficulty walking.

A 55-year-old man who has been alcohol-free for 3 years continues to have severe ANTEROGRADE AMNESIA — he cannot remember new information for more than a few minutes. He confabulates to fill in the gaps. His cognition is otherwise relatively intact.
distractors_rationale: ALCOHOLIC HALLUCINOSIS (B). Key features: (1) AUDITORY HALLUCINATIONS (usually threatening, persecutory voices); (2) CLEAR CONSCIOUSNESS (intact orientation, alert) — this DISTINGUISHES it from delirium tremens; (3) Onset: 12-24 hours after last drink (sometimes up to 48 hours); (4) Duration: days to weeks (can become chronic in some cases — 'chronic alcoholic hallucinosis'); (5) No significant autonomic instability (unlike DTs). Management: benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide reducing regimen) + antipsychotic (low-dose risperidone/olanzapine) if symptoms severe. The key differential is DTs (delirium) — in DTs, the patient is CONFUSED and has AUTONOMIC HYPERACTIVITY.

DELIRIUM TREMENS (C). DTs is a MEDICAL EMERGENCY (mortality ~5%). Features: (1) Onset: 48-96 hours after last drink (peak day 3); (2) CONFUSION (disoriented, fluctuating consciousness); (3) Visual hallucinations (insects, animals — 'formication' — feeling of crawling insects on skin); (4) AUTONOMIC HYPERACTIVITY (tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, diaphoresis); (5) Tremor, agitation, insomnia. Management: (1) ADMIT to medical ward/HDU; (2) HIGH-DOSE BENZODIAZEPINES (diazepam 10-20mg IV front-loading or chlordiazepoxide reducing regimen increased doses); (3) IV thiamine (Pabrinex); (4) Correct electrolyte abnormalities; (5) Monitor for complications: aspiration, arrhythmias, seizures, rhabdomyolysis, AKI.

ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL SEIZURE — 'RUM FIT' (A). Features: (1) GENERALISED TONIC-CLONIC (not focal — if focal, consider underlying structural lesion); (2) Single or brief cluster (status epilepticus is rare); (3) Onset: 12-48 hours after last drink (peak 24 hours); (4) About 2-5% of alcohol withdrawal cases; (5) 30-50% of those with a first seizure will develop DTs if untreated. Management: benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide IV/lorazepam IV for acute seizure, chlordiazepoxide reducing regimen for prevention). Phenytoin is NOT indicated for alcohol withdrawal seizures. Long-term anticonvulsants are NOT needed unless there is a separate epilepsy diagnosis.

WERNICKE'S ENCEPHALOPATHY (D). A medical emergency caused by THIAMINE (B1) DEFICIENCY in chronic alcohol dependence with poor nutrition. CLASSIC TRIAD (only 30% present with all three): (1) Confusion (global confusion, disorientation, inattention); (2) ATAXIA (gait disturbance, unable to walk without support); (3) OPHTHALMOPLEGIA (nystagmus, lateral rectus palsy, conjugate gaze palsy). MANAGEMENT: IMMEDIATE IV THIAMINE (Pabrinex — one pair containing thiamine 250mg + riboflavin + pyridoxine + nicotinamide IV BD/TDS for 3-5 days). Oral thiamine is INADEQUATE for treatment. Untreated Wernicke's progresses to Korsakoff's syndrome in ~80% of survivors. Wernicke's can be triggered by a HIGH GLUCOSE LOAD (e.g., starting IV dextrose before thiamine — the glucose depletes remaining thiamine — can cause irreversible brain damage).

KORSAKOFF'S SYNDROME (E). A chronic amnestic syndrome resulting from untreated Wernicke's encephalopathy. Features: (1) SEVERE ANTEROGRADE AMNESIA (inability to form new memories) — the hallmark; (2) VARIABLE RETROGRADE AMNESIA; (3) CONFABULATION (fabricating answers to fill memory gaps — 'honestly lying'); (4) OTHER COGNITIVE FUNCTIONS relatively preserved; (5) APATHY, lack of insight. Pathophysiology: lesions in the MAMMILLARY BODIES, DORSOMEDIAL NUCLEUS OF THE THALAMUS, and periaqueductal grey. MRI: may show atrophy of mammillary bodies, thalamic lesions. Treatment: (1) THIAMINE (IM/IV) — may prevent progression but does NOT reverse established Korsakoff's; (2) SUPPORTIVE — residential care, memory aids, supervision. Prognosis: about 20-30% recover partially; 20-30% recover fully but with mild memory deficits; most remain severely impaired and require long-term care.
teaching_point: Alcohol withdrawal spectrum — MRCPsych classic: Mild withdrawal (6-12h): tremor, sweating, anxiety. Seizures (12-48h): generalised tonic-clonic. Hallucinosis (12-48h): auditory hallucinations, CLEAR consciousness. Delirium tremens (48-96h): confusion, autonomic hyperactivity, hallucinations — MEDICAL EMERGENCY. Wernicke's: confusion + ataxia + ophthalmoplegia — treat with IV thiamine IMMEDIATELY. Korsakoff's: severe anterograde amnesia + confabulation — irreversible. CAGEWORD: 'Confusion' (DTs), 'Ataxia' (Wernicke's), 'Gaps' (Korsakoff's), 'Eye signs' (Wernicke's), 'Wobbling' (ataxia), 'Ophthalmoplegia' (Wernicke's), 'Rum fits' (seizures), 'Delerium' (DTs).
source: NICE CG115: Alcohol dependence; BNF; Ewusie JE et al. (2023) Cochrane review

stem: A 56-year-old man with no history of epilepsy develops his FIRST generalised tonic-clonic seizure on day 2 of an inpatient alcohol detoxification. He has been drinking >20 units/day for 20 years. His SADQ score is 38. He was started on chlordiazepoxide 20mg QDS yesterday. Observations: HR 88, BP 128/78, Temp 36.8°C. The seizure lasted 90 seconds and resolved spontaneously. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Start phenytoin 300mg daily for seizure prophylaxis
Increase the chlordiazepoxide dose (this is a breakthrough withdrawal seizure — insufficient benzodiazepine cover) and ensure IV thiamine is given
Transfer to ICU for status epilepticus monitoring
Perform an urgent CT head and refer to neurology
Start levetiracetam 500mg BD
distractors_rationale: Phenytoin is NOT effective for alcohol withdrawal seizures. Benzodiazepines (which work via GABA potentiation) are the appropriate treatment. Chronic antiepileptics are only indicated if the patient has a SEPARATE epilepsy diagnosis (not alcohol-withdrawal seizures alone).

CORRECT. An alcohol withdrawal seizure despite chlordiazepoxide 20mg QDS indicates INSUFFICIENT BENZODIAZEPINE COVERAGE. The patient has SEVERE alcohol dependence (SADQ 38) and needs a HIGHER DOSE of chlordiazepoxide. Management: (1) INCREASE chlordiazepoxide (e.g., to 30-40mg QDS) to achieve adequate sedation and seizure control; (2) Ensure IV thiamine (Pabrinex) is given — withdrawal seizures can also be triggered by thiamine deficiency; (3) Monitor for further seizures and progression to DTs; (4) Check electrolytes (K+, Mg2+, Ca2+ — hypomagnesaemia can cause seizures). Single alcohol withdrawal seizures do NOT require neuroimaging unless there is: FOCAL onset, prolonged post-ictal state, focal neurological signs, head injury, or first seizure at an age >40 with risk factors for structural lesions.
Status epilepticus (continuous seizure >5 min or multiple without recovery) is not present — the seizure resolved spontaneously. HDU/ICU is not needed.
CT head is not indicated for a first generalised alcohol withdrawal seizure. If there were focal signs, prolonged confusion, or head injury — then yes.
Levetiracetam is not indicated — alcohol withdrawal seizures are treated with BENZODIAZEPINES (GABAergic).
teaching_point: Alcohol withdrawal seizures — management: (1) ACUTE SEIZURE: IV lorazepam 2-4mg or IV diazepam 5-10mg if seizing. (2) PROPHYLAXIS: adequate chlordiazepoxide (or equivalent) reducing regimen. The dosage should be HIGH ENOUGH to prevent seizures. (3) CONTEXT: alcohol withdrawal seizures are a sign of SEVERE DEPENDENCE — they predict DTs. (4) MONITORING: CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment) every 2-4 hours. (5) ELECTROLYTES: check and correct K+, Mg2+, Ca2+. (6) THIAMINE: IV Pabrinex essential. (7) DO NOT: start long-term anticonvulsants (phenytoin, valproate, levetiracetam) — they do not prevent alcohol withdrawal seizures. (8) IMAGING: only if first seizure, focal seizure, prolonged post-ictal confusion, head injury, or >40 with risk factors. The mnemonic for ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL SEIZURES: 'B-1-2-3-D': Benzodiazepines first-line; 1 = check electrolytes (K+, Mg2+); 2 = two conditions to exclude (head injury, other causes); 3 = three risk factors (SADQ >30, previous seizures/DTs, high daily intake); D = DTs risk.
source: NICE CG115; BNF; Schuckit MA (2014) Alcohol withdrawal seizures

stem: A 32-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder and treatment-resistant depression has been on sertraline 150mg daily, quetiapine 150mg nocte, and PRN lorazepam. She presents with severe agitation, confusion, tachycardia (120bpm), hyperreflexia, and inducible ankle clonus. Temp 37.5°C. BP 155/90. She is on no other serotonergic medications. What is the MOST likely diagnosis and immediate management?
options: NMS — stop quetiapine, start dantrolene
SEROTONIN SYNDROME — stop sertraline (and consider if she has taken additional serotonergic agents), supportive care, consider cyproheptadine
Anticholinergic delirium — stop lorazepam
Malignant catatonia — start lorazepam challenge
BPD crisis with dissociation — reassurance and PRN lorazepam
distractors_rationale: NMS presents with LEAD-PIPE RIGIDITY (not clonus), bradyreflexia (not hyperreflexia), and extremely elevated CK. Clonus is the HALLMARK of serotonin syndrome. The presence of clonus + hyperreflexia + agitation + autonomic instability strongly favours serotonin syndrome.

CORRECT. This patient has SEROTONIN SYNDROME (Hunter Toxicity Criteria). The HUNTER criteria require ONE of: (1) Spontaneous clonus; (2) Inducible clonus + agitation/diaphoresis; (3) Ocular clonus + agitation/diaphoresis; (4) Tremor + hyperreflexia; (5) Hypertonia + temp >38°C + ocular/inducible clonus. This patient has inducible clonus + agitation + hyperreflexia + autonomic instability. But: SEROTONIN SYNDROME typically occurs within 6-24 hours of serotonergic drug exposure. Sertraline 150mg plus quetiapine 150mg alone is UNLIKELY to cause serotonin syndrome (quetiapine is a weak 5-HT antagonist). The question HINTS that she may have taken ADDITIONAL serotonergic drugs (possibility of overdose or other medications). Emergency management: (1) STOP all serotonergic drugs; (2) SUPPORTIVE CARE (IV fluids, cooling, monitoring); (3) In MODERATE cases: consider CYPROHEPTADINE (5-HT2A antagonist) — 12mg initially, then 2mg Q2h up to 32mg/day; (4) In SEVERE cases (hyperthermia >41°C, severe agitation, autonomic instability): IV benzodiazepines (diazepam), sedation, ICU admission.
Lorazepam alone would not cause anticholinergic delirium — it is a benzodiazepine (GABAergic), not anticholinergic.

Malignant catatonia presents with rigidity, mutism, posturing, stupor, and autonomic instability — NOT with hyperreflexia and clonus. A lorazepam challenge (1-2mg IV) can differentiate: if symptoms resolve, it supports catatonia. However, the presence of clonus + hyperreflexia favours serotonin syndrome.
This is clearly an organic state, not BPD dissociation.
teaching_point: Serotonin syndrome vs NMS vs malignant catatonia — THE MRCPsych DIFFERENTIAL: SEROTONIN SYNDROME — CLONUS (spontaneous/inducible/ocular) is PATHOGNOMONIC. Hyperreflexia, tremour, myoclonus, autonomic instability, hyperthermia. Rapid onset (hours). Cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist). NMS — LEAD-PIPE RIGIDITY without clonus. Bradykinesia/Bradyreflexia. Extremely high CK (>10,000). Autonomic instability. Gradual onset (1-3 days). Dantrolene/bromocriptine. MALIGNANT CATATONIA — Rigidity + mutism/posturing/stupor + autonomic instability. Can be indistinguishable from NMS. Lorazepam challenge is diagnostic (and therapeutic). ECT is most effective. The HUNTER CRITERIA (2003) are more sensitive and specific for serotonin syndrome than the original Sternbach criteria. CLONUS IS THE KEY — if clonus is present, it is serotonin syndrome until proven otherwise. The incidence of serotonin syndrome is increasing due to polypharmacy (SSRI + SNRI + MAOI + lithium + tramadol + linezolid + St John's Wort + MDMA). The STERNNBACH criteria: (1) Recent serotonergic drug; (2) ≥3 of: mental state changes, agitation, myoclonus, hyperreflexia, diaphoresis, shivering, tremour, diarrhoea, incordination, fever.
source: Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria; Sternbach H (1991) J Clin Psychopharmacol; Maudsley PG
